title: Profitable Schemes
hints: each crime is either included in the scheme or not, and including it costs members from a shared budget of n while contributing profit - that's 0/1 knapsack with a members budget, but what do you do with the profit dimension?

define dp[members][p] as the number of schemes using at most 'members' people that achieve profit exactly p (or at least p if you cap p at minProfit) - the key trick is capping profit at minProfit, since any profit that reaches or exceeds minProfit is equally profitable

for each crime with cost g and gain pr, update dp[members][p] += dp[members - g][max(0, p - pr)] for members from n down to g, and p from minProfit down to 0 - use max(0, p - pr) so that overshooting minProfit still lands you at the 'already profitable' bucket p=0's counterpart, i.e. clamp the reduced profit index at 0
initialize dp[members][0] = 1 for every members from 0 to n (0 crimes chosen, 0 profit, always exactly 1 way: choose nothing), since the empty scheme is a valid starting point for every member budget

after processing every crime, sum dp[members][minProfit] over every members from 0 to n (or just read dp[n][minProfit] if profit was tracked as 'at least minProfit' throughout) - remember to apply the modulo after every addition
commonMistakes: forgetting to clamp the profit index at 0 when a crime's profit alone meets or exceeds the remaining minProfit needed, causing an out-of-bounds negative index
not initializing dp[members][0] = 1 for all members up front, which undercounts every scheme since the empty selection is a valid base case at every member budget
forgetting the modulo, or applying it only at the very end instead of after each accumulation, causing overflow in fixed-width integer types

content.problemStatement:
A crew has `n` available members. There's a list of possible crimes, where
each crime requires a certain number of members to pull off (`group[i]`)
and yields a certain profit (`profit[i]`). A "scheme" is any subset of
crimes (including none at all) whose total member requirement does not
exceed `n`. A scheme is "profitable" if its total profit is at least
`minProfit`.

**Return the number of different profitable schemes, modulo 1000000007.**

Two schemes are different if they include a different subset of crimes.
notes: minProfit is 0 (the empty scheme alone already counts as profitable)
n is smaller than every crime's group requirement (only the empty scheme, if profitable, counts)
every crime can be included at once without exceeding n

sampleTestCases.explanation: the profitable schemes are {crime 1 alone} (uses 2 members, profit 3) and {crime 0, crime 1} (uses 4 members, profit 5); {crime 0 alone} only makes profit 2, which is below minProfit
every non-empty subset of the three crimes fits within 10 members and already clears a profit of 5, giving 7 profitable schemes (2^3 - 1 non-empty subsets)
only the scheme using that single crime is profitable

optimal.pattern: knapsack (0/1, two dimensions - members used capped at n, and profit tracked up to a cap of minProfit since any profit beyond minProfit is equally 'good enough')

bruteForce.approach: try every subset of crimes (2^k possibilities), check whether its total group usage fits within n and its total profit is at least minProfit, and count the ones that qualify
